lead: A programmable logic device (PLD) is an IC whose logic function you set after manufacture. Instead of drawing new masks, you store connections or truth tables in programmable cells. This makes PLDs useful for prototypes, low-volume products, education and glue logic. FPGA (field-programmable gate array) is the largest PLD family: it builds arbitrary logic from lookup tables, flip-flops, routing and I/O blocks. This chapter explains the PLD families, the blocks inside an FPGA, and how SRAM, flash and antifuse programming differ at block level.
prereq: You need: modelling styles for the synthesizable Verilog subset, and Boolean functions in sum-of-products form from digital electronics.

blocks.text: Programmable logic devices (PLDs) let you set a logic function after the chip is made. A masked gate array is fixed once its metal masks are made; a PLD stores its connections in programmable elements. In a programmable logic array (PLA), both the AND plane and the OR plane are programmable, so each output is an OR of selected product terms. A product term is one AND of input literals, where a literal is a variable or its complement. A programmable array logic (PAL) keeps the AND plane programmable and fixes the OR plane; it is simpler and faster. Programmable inversion lets an input or output be used in true or complemented form. Expander logic feeds extra product terms into a macrocell without using output pins. A macrocell is the programmable logic cell of a complex PLD (CPLD); it contains product-term logic, a register and polarity control. A CPLD joins several PAL-like blocks with a central interconnect. A mask-programmable gate array (MPGA) is programmed by custom wiring masks, so its function is fixed at fabrication. An FPGA is field-programmable: the user loads a configuration after packaging.

blocks.text: An FPGA logic cell is built around a lookup table (LUT) and a flip-flop. An n-input LUT stores 2ⁿ truth-table bits; a multiplexer chosen by the n inputs selects one bit. A 4-input LUT has 16 bits and can implement any 4-variable Boolean function. The flip-flop after the LUT stores the result for sequential logic; a bypass multiplexer selects combinational or registered output. A logic block packs several LUTs, flip-flops and carry logic. In Xilinx (now AMD) FPGAs it is the configurable logic block (CLB); Intel FPGAs call it a logic array block (LAB). Not every FPGA uses LUTs: the Actel (now Microchip) antifuse families built their logic module from multiplexers; the ACT 1 module is three 2:1 multiplexers and an OR gate, and a function is made by tying its inputs to signals, 0 or 1. Input/output blocks (IOBs) connect pads to the array with registers and drive strength. Routing runs through horizontal and vertical channels; a switch box at each crossing connects wire segments. Routing delay often dominates. Block RAM (BRAM) gives on-chip memory. DSP slices give fast multiply-accumulate. Clock management blocks such as phase-locked loops (PLLs) clean and multiply clocks. All these choices are set by configuration memory.

blocks.where: N<sub>LUT</sub> is the number of configuration bits in an n-input LUT; n is the number of LUT inputs.

blocks.text: FPGA programming is stored in configuration memory. SRAM-based FPGAs use volatile SRAM cells that drive pass transistors. They lose configuration at power-off, so a bitstream must be reloaded from flash or a host. Their advantage is unlimited reprogramming and standard CMOS fabrication. Flash-based FPGAs store charge on a floating gate; they keep configuration without power and can be reprogrammed, but need special process steps. Antifuse FPGAs blow a one-time link; they are non-volatile and hard to reverse, used where radiation or security matters. Older PLDs and CPLDs used EPROM or EEPROM cells, which are erased by UV light or electrically. Some syllabi call this choice the switching (or programming) technology. At block level, an SRAM cell, a floating-gate transistor or a blown antifuse controls a switch. Synthesis maps Verilog to LUTs; packing groups them; placement and routing choose sites and wires; bitstream generation writes the memory. See floorplanning, placement and routing for ASIC placement and routing, and IP cores and soft-core processors for reusing soft cores.

sections.h3: Implementing logic with ROM, PAL and PLA

blocks.text: A ROM implements logic by storing the truth table: n inputs address 2<sup>n</sup> words, and each output is one bit of the word, so the size is 2<sup>n</sup> × m bits for m outputs. It needs no minimisation, but its size doubles with every input. A PLA needs the functions in sum-of-products form; its size is set by the number of distinct product terms, and outputs share any term they have in common. A PAL also needs sum-of-products form, but each output has its own fixed set of AND gates, so a shared term is built twice.

A PLA is specified by a programming table: one row per product term, a 1, 0 or – for each input (true, complemented or not used), and a 1 under each output whose OR gate uses that term. The second worked example fills one in.

figure.caption: The worked example’s LUT. Its 16 configuration bits hold the truth table of f = A·B + C·D, one bit per input address, and the inputs drive a 16:1 multiplexer that reads one bit out. For A = 1, B = 1, C = 0, D = 1 it reads address 1101 = 13, which holds 1.

examples.question: A 4-input LUT implements f = A·B + C·D. (a) How many configuration bits does it need? (b) Find f for A=1, B=1, C=0, D=1. (c) How many LUTs are needed for 3,000 such functions if 15% of LUTs are lost to packing?
steps: A 4-input LUT has 2⁴ = 16 truth-table entries. Each entry stores one configuration bit. Configuration bits = 16.
For A = 1, B = 1, C = 0, D = 1 the inputs form the address ABCD = 1101 = 13. A·B = 1 and C·D = 0, so f = 1 OR 0 = 1, the bit stored at address 13.
Useful fraction after packing = 1 − 0.15 = 0.85. Required LUTs = 3,000 ÷ 0.85 = 3529.4. Round up because LUT count is an integer: 3530 LUTs.
examples.answer: The LUT needs 16 configuration bits, f = 1 for A=1, B=1, C=0, D=1, and 3530 LUTs are needed after 15% packing loss.

examples.question: Implement F1 = AB + AC′ and F2 = AB + BC with (a) a ROM, (b) a PLA and (c) a PAL. Give the ROM size and truth table, the PLA programming table, and the number of AND gates (product terms) each programmable device needs.
steps: (a) Three inputs address 2³ = 8 words; two outputs give 2 bits per word. ROM size = 8 × 2 = 16 bits.
So F1 = Σm(4, 6, 7) and F2 = Σm(3, 6, 7); the ROM stores these eight words.
(b) The distinct product terms are P1 = AB, P2 = AC′ and P3 = BC. F1 = P1 + P2 and F2 = P1 + P3 share P1, so the PLA needs only 3 AND gates.
PLA table (inputs A B C, outputs F1 F2): P1 = AB → 1 1 –, 1 1. P2 = AC′ → 1 – 0, 1 0. P3 = BC → – 1 1, 0 1.
(c) In a PAL each output has its own AND gates, so AB is built twice: F1 uses AB and AC′, F2 uses AB and BC, 4 AND gates in all, and the PAL must offer at least 2 terms per output.
Check one row: ABC = 110 gives AB = 1, so F1 = F2 = 1 in every form, matching word 6 of the ROM.
examples.answer: ROM: 8 × 2 = 16 bits, F1 = Σm(4, 6, 7), F2 = Σm(3, 6, 7). PLA: 3 product terms (AB shared). PAL: 4 product terms, 2 per output.

traps: An n-input LUT is not an n-input gate; it stores 2ⁿ truth-table bits and behaves like a small memory.
An n-input LUT needs 2ⁿ configuration bits, not n bits; a 4-input LUT needs 16 bits.

In a PAL the OR plane is fixed, so each output gets a fixed number of product terms — count them per output, not as a shared pool. In a PLA the product terms are shared, and each output ORs a programmable subset of them.
SRAM FPGA configuration memory is volatile like user SRAM, but it holds the logic configuration, not program data.
Routing and switch-box delay can dominate, so equal LUT counts do not guarantee equal speed.

quiz.q: What is a product term in a PLA?
quiz.a: A product term is an AND of selected input literals, true or complemented; each PLA output is an OR of selected product terms.

quiz.q: Why does an n-input LUT need 2ⁿ configuration bits?
quiz.a: It must store one output bit for every one of the 2ⁿ input combinations, and a multiplexer selects the addressed bit.

quiz.q: A 5-input LUT implements a Boolean function. How many configuration bits does it store?
An FPGA has 4,800 6-input LUTs. 20% are lost to packing. How many useful LUTs remain?
Why can two FPGAs with the same number of LUTs run at different clock speeds?
quiz.a: Routing architecture, switch-box delays, wire lengths, clock networks and placement affect the critical-path delay; LUT count alone does not fix speed.

quiz.q: Contrast SRAM and antifuse configuration at block level.
quiz.a: SRAM uses a volatile memory cell driving a pass transistor, is reloaded at power-up and is reprogrammable. Antifuse blows a one-time link, is non-volatile and is not reprogrammable.

quiz.q: Name four kinds of block inside an FPGA.
quiz.a: Logic blocks of LUTs and flip-flops (CLBs), programmable routing with switch boxes, I/O blocks (IOBs) at the edge, and block RAM, DSP slices or clock managers.

quiz.q: How many bits does a ROM need to implement four functions of 5 inputs?

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern FPGAs add high-speed transceivers, memory controllers, AI DSP arrays and hardened processor cores, so the fabric is only part of the chip. Partial reconfiguration lets one region change while the rest runs. Open-source toolchains now synthesize and place small FPGA designs. Search for FPGA bitstream format, LUT mapping and partial reconfiguration.
